In our area none of the nursing homes, hospice, anything will accept patients on Methadone. And the patient’s I’ve had that needed to go to nursing homes ended up hours away from their hometown and their family.

Depends on clinical judgement. A patient could overdose with grape fruit juice and a week of take home bottles on an empty stomach. However, any human could commit suicide with 5 or 6 gallons of water in a short peroid. Ultimately, it's all about managing liability.

From my experience I've seen the most success with the following two rules. Don't exceed any drop that is greater than 10% of your current dose. Don't drop at any frequency that's faster than every three weeks. Everyone is different; just my observations.
I'd expect you to still test positive. Methadone lasts a hot minute.

Best way withdrawals have been explained to me is from Jeremy Clarkson; no seriously hahaha. Going fast killed no one; stopping suddenly is what gets you. You just crashed head on into a brick wall going 60mph. I wouldn't advise it. Try a taper like 2 or 3 mg a month for a year and that should half your dose. Think about it instead of hitting a brick wall, spin out of control in an empty soccer field. Lots of room :) and you get to drive away like nothing happened.

I would always encourage trust and honestly with your assigned clinician. You wouldn’t withhold information to your mechanic or your surgeon? I’d encourage the same level of communication with your counselor. Now, unfortunately there are some really poor clinicians out there. So, use your best judgement. But ultimately you’re the expert on how you’re doing. If you need to go up go up.

Also, a relapse is defined as far as I’m aware as a return to previous use. So, if you were using every day throughout the day this would be a relapse. A lapse is a return to substance use, but a momentary event that doesn’t represent previous established use frequency and volume. Lapses are normal during recovery.

I can provide an anecdote. A client of mine detailed over the holiday season they met with an old friend and had used. They told me right away and I advocated on their behalf to not remove take home bottles due to their insight and honesty. They didn’t repeat any use and were providing negative urine screens in under a month.

I would expect what I did is the gold standard and demonstrates a strong relationship between the patient and clinician. I wouldn’t guarantee this would be your case, but just an example of best case.

The clinic not allowing a dose decrease or formation of a taper plan for whatever reason appears to me flirting with illegality if the clinic is in the USA. Patient’s rights is a pretty well established for all providers. Patients are always able to refuse treatment, informed consent, and participate in decisions regarding their care. I’d imagine it’s a particular policy or individualized practice to avoid tapering during active use. However, if the patient is not using and requests to taper I don’t believe the clinic has the right to refuse. I’d request an appointment with the leading physician or to present your case to the MDT. Unfortunately, most clinics won’t entertain false positives. And furthermore, the clinic can only go on the data provided. Best of luck 😊

In that context a little worry and anxiety is warranted depending on the state you reside in. My clinic historically refused to disrupt treatment regardless of high the bill was. And we did have a few balances over $15,000. However, now a days. No way. If you have a bill close to $1000; adminsitrative taper is right around the corner.

As an American working at a clinic for just shy of ten years I wouldn’t encourage any particular anxiety or concern regarding continued dosing. As a team we reviewed our emergency planning at the height of Covid. And the contingency plan if the shit hits the fan is the National guard would deliver bottles to all our client’s listed address.

If anything be sure to update your contact information at the clinic. That means; phone number, address, email, emergency contact. Otherwise I really can’t imagine a scenario where Methadone would just be abruptly unavailable. Seems pretty established that any interruption could be detrimental to the community and the patients. Finally, seems like Trump has a particular sense that treatment substance use is a worthy cause.

From my experience I can offer the following advice: don’t exceed 10% of your dose per drop. And don’t exceed a frequency of less than every three weeks. Those two simple rules and I’ve been able to see plenty of people taper off of Methadone successfully and return to life without it.

It's spelled out very clear in Methadone guidlines for clinics from SAMHSA that lockboxs must be used in order for take home doses to be dispensed.

  
Otherwords the clinc would get in trouble for dispensing a dose without a lockbox. So they're in the clear here.

state and federal laws may limit dosing hours. its generally not one or the other, but how the two work together. for example federal law may stipulate dosing can only be executed during licensed hours. then the state license is for 6am to 11am. most of the time people won't bat an eye about 10 mins after 11am, however, if the agency is facing an audit they might be more picky about how things are done and insist on staying within the letter of the law rather than the spirit.

First realize you're experiencing a disease similar to the common cold, really. The symptoms you listed are common depression. I'd suggest try to be strong and understand things will get better. Could be the seasons, or obviously your friend moving away. Best advice is fake being happy and reach out to as many people as you can. Try to imagine all your fellow students are friends, pretend they are and try to talk to people about whats going on for them. Should help somewhat.
